what_its_for: Granisetron is used to prevent nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or surgery. It works by blocking signals in your body that trigger the feeling of nausea.
how_to_take: Granisetron comes in several forms: a tablet or liquid you swallow, a patch you wear on your skin, or an injection given by a healthcare provider. Take the tablet or liquid with or without food. If you are using the skin patch (Sancuso), apply it to clean, dry, hairless skin on your upper arm at least 24 to 48 hours before your chemotherapy starts. Press the patch firmly in place and keep it on for up to 7 days. Do not cut the patch. If you receive the injection form (Sustol), it will be given to you by a nurse or doctor.
dosing: The usual adult dose of the tablet is 1 mg taken twice a day (once before chemotherapy and once 12 hours later), or 2 mg taken once before chemotherapy. Your doctor will decide the right dose and timing for you based on your treatment. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose of the tablet or liquid, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is close to the time of your chemotherapy or radiation treatment. If it has been a long time since you missed the dose, skip it and talk to your doctor or nurse. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. For the skin patch, apply it as soon as you remember if you still have treatments coming up, and call your doctor for guidance.
storage: Store tablets and liquid at room temperature, away from heat, light, and moisture. Keep the liquid form tightly closed. Store skin patches in their sealed pouches at room temperature until you are ready to use them. Keep all forms of this medication out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medication down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking granisetron, as it may worsen dizziness or drowsiness. Be careful driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid exposing the skin patch to direct sunlight or heat sources such as heating pads, electric blankets, or tanning beds while wearing it, as heat can increase the amount of medicine absorbed into your body. Do not apply sunscreen or lotion directly on top of the patch.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: a fast, slow, or irregular heartbeat or chest pain; severe constipation or stomach pain; a severe headache; sudden confusion, agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shaking, or muscle twitching (these could be signs of a rare but serious condition called serotonin syndrome); signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing; skin irritation or blistering where the patch is applied; or if your nausea and vomiting are not being controlled.
when_it_works: Granisetron starts working within about 1 to 3 hours when taken by mouth. It works best when taken before your chemotherapy or radiation treatment rather than after nausea has already started. The skin patch takes about 24 to 48 hours to reach full effect, which is why it must be applied in advance. The injection form works very quickly because it is given directly by your healthcare team before treatment.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): Granisetron is generally safe for older adults, but they may be more sensitive to side effects like constipation or dizziness. Use with caution and report any unusual symptoms to your doctor. Pregnant women: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks before prescribing this medication. Breastfeeding women: It is not fully known if granisetron passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while taking this medication. Children: The safety and dosing for children depend on their age, weight, and condition. Always follow the dose your child's doctor has prescribed. Patients with liver problems: Granisetron is usually safe for people with liver problems, but your doctor may monitor you more closely.
